overview.body:
**Hati** (*hati*) — Moon-Chaser, Chaos · The Hater, Son of the Fame-Wolf — is the wolf the Edda sets running after the moon: Hati Hróðvitnisson, son of the fame-wolf [[fenrir|Fenrir]], who runs before the sun and at the heels of [[mani|Máni]], and who is fated to seize his quarry out of the sky when [[ragnarok|Ragnarǫk]] comes.[^1]

His name is one of the most transparent theonyms in the corpus: Old Norse *hati* is the ordinary agent noun 'hater, enemy', from the verb *hata*, 'to hate' — the wolf is called, simply, 'the Hater'.[^3] His dossier is thin and exact: one verse of *Grímnismál* names him and his father, Snorri's Gylfaginning gives him his quarry and his foreknown success, and *Völuspá* supplies the Ironwood kennel he springs from, where the old giantess breeds Fenrir's brood and 'from all of them comes one in particular, a snatcher of the moon in a troll's skin'.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Hati** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name; the mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2, a statement about orthography and never about the figure. The project holds no domain for this name: the plain-ASCII **hati.com** is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 12 (Skǫll and Hati; Mánagarmr) and 51 (Ragnarǫk), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Grímnismál 39 and Völuspá 39–40 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. hati, hata.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Hati**, always with the patronymic **Hróðvitnisson**, 'son of Hróðvitnir'. It is the ordinary Old Norse masculine agent noun *hati*, 'hater, enemy', formed on the verb *hata*, 'to hate' — the same Proto-Germanic word (*hatōjan-) that gives English *hate*.[^1] The etymology is not disputed; the name means what it says. The patronymic fixes his pedigree: *Hróðvitnir*, 'fame-wolf', is a poetic heiti of [[fenrir|Fenrir]], so the verse that names Hati names him as the bound wolf's son.[^2]

The ASCII form is not a compromise here: normalized Old Norse *Hati* is already written in plain ASCII letters. There is no diacritic, no thorn or eth, no vowel-length mark for the early domain-name system to have stripped. The name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule — the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses. Note also what the name lacks: unlike most Old Norse masculine theonyms (Baldr, Hermóðr), it carries no nominative *-r*, because it is a weak-declension agent noun ending in a stem vowel.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **h** → **H** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

The project holds no domain for this name: **hati.com** is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release; this temple claims no domain.

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. hati, hata, Hróðvitnir.
Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. hati; de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. hata.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈhɑ.ti/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **H-** — Voiceless glottal fricative [h], as in English *hat*; Old Norse initial h is fully sounded
- **-a-** — Short open back unrounded [ɑ], held brief — Old Norse short a, not the long á
- **-ti** — Voiceless dental stop [t] and short front [i]; the second syllable is unstressed and clipped

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'HAH-tih' — two short syllables, stress on the first, with plain short vowels and no final nominative -r.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Hati Hróðvitnisson, the moon-chasing wolf of Grímnismál and Gylfaginning
- **Common noun** — hati, 'hater, enemy', the agent noun of hata, 'to hate'
- **English cognate** — hate, the same Proto-Germanic word, *hatōjan-
- **Modern Icelandic** — Hati, unchanged in spelling since the medieval manuscripts

Hati is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing ASCII cannot carry: no diacritic, no thorn or eth, no length mark. The name's distinctiveness is semantic, not orthographic — it is the verb 'to hate' given legs and set after the moon.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.

domains.body:
**Hati** is catalogued under the domain 'Moon-Chaser, Chaos' — and the sources earn both terms of it.[^1]

### The Moon-Chaser

His sole function in the corpus is pursuit: Grímnismál sets him running before the sun, Snorri assigns him the moon as his quarry, and Völuspá's 'snatcher of the moon in a troll's skin' is the role the handbooks read as his. The chase is his whole mythology.

### Chaos

He belongs to the forces the gods cannot bind: bred in the Ironwood from [[fenrir|Fenrir]]'s own line, he is one of the certainties of [[ragnarok|Ragnarǫk]] — the catch Snorri says simply 'will happen'. His chaos is not randomness but inevitability: order pursued.

### The Eclipse-Wolf

The handbooks read the chase as the sky's own etiology: when the wolf draws close to his quarry, the moon darkens — the medieval North's explanation of the lunar eclipse, and the reason the figure endures in every account of the northern sky-myths.[^2]

### The Fenrir-Complex

Hati never acts alone in the tradition: he is one face of the apocalyptic wolf-complex that also includes [[skoll|Skǫll]], Mánagarmr, [[garmr|Garmr]], and Fenrir himself — the kennel of the world's ending.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 12, trans. Faulkes (1987); Grímnismál 39 and Völuspá 39–40, trans. Larrington (2014).

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hati, Skǫll; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sköll.

symbols.body:
The iconography of Hati is narrative and celestial — the corpus gives him no regalia, but the chase itself fixed a small set of images:[^1]

- **The running wolf** — pursuit without rest: the sky itself read as a hunt that has never once paused
- **The fleeing moon** — [[mani|Máni]]'s measured course reinterpreted as flight: what astronomy calls a path, the poem calls terror
- **Járnviðr, the Ironwood** — the eastern forest where the old giantess breeds Fenrir's brood: chaos with an address, growing older by the year
- **The darkened sky** — Völuspá's 'the sunshine turns black in the summers after': the eclipse and the world's ending written in one image
- **The troll's skin** — the seeress's phrase for the moon-snatcher's guise: the wolf-shape worn as a monster's garment over a name the poem withholds[^2]

sources.citation: Völuspá 39–40 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sköll.

mythology.body:
Hati's mythology is a single image carried by a handful of verses: a wolf, a moon, and a chase that ends only with the world.

### The Pair Before Heaven (Grímnismál 39)

The name's one poetic attestation comes in [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s great catalogue of the cosmos in *Grímnismál*: '[[skoll|Skǫll]] is the name of the wolf who follows the bright-faced god to the sheltering wood; but the other is Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, who runs before the bright bride of heaven.' The bright bride of heaven is [[sol|Sól]]; the wolf who runs before her is on the heels of the moon that travels ahead of her. In four lines the Edda converts the machinery of the sky into a hunt.[^1]

### Snorri's System (Gylfaginning 12)

Snorri systematizes the verse. When Gangleri asks why the sun hurries so — 'she speeds as if she were afraid' — High One answers that the one who seeks her is right behind her. Two wolves do the work of the heavens: Skǫll chases the sun and will catch her, and 'the other wolf is called Hati Hróðvitnisson; he runs in front of her and wants to catch the moon — and that is what will happen.'[^2]

### Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound

In the same chapter Snorri names the mightiest of the brood: Mánagarmr, 'moon-hound' — 'he will be filled with the flesh of all who die, and he will swallow the moon and spatter the sky and all the air with blood.' Whether Mánagarmr is Hati under a second name or a third wolf beside the pair, the manuscripts leave open; Simek and Lindow record the identification as probable but unprovable.[^3]

### The Brood of the Ironwood (Völuspá 39–40)

The seeress supplies the kennel: 'In the east sat the old one in the Ironwood and bred there Fenrir's brood; from all of them comes one in particular, a snatcher of the moon in a troll's skin. He gorges on the life of doomed men, reddens the gods' dwellings with red blood; the sunshine turns black in the summers after.' The poem names no name — but the *tungls tjúgari*, the 'snatcher of the moon', is the role Grímnismál and Snorri assign to Hati.[^1]

### The Catch (Gylfaginning 51 · Völuspá)

The ending is shared by every witness: when [[ragnarok|Ragnarǫk]] comes, the running stops — Skǫll takes the sun, Hati takes the moon, Fenrir swallows Óðinn, and the bright stars vanish from the sky. The Edda's cosmology is built so that the nightly order of the heavens is only an interval: the long meanwhile between the start of the chase and its foreknown end.[^2]

Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 12 and 51, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Mánagarm; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sköll.

syncretism.body:
Hati has no cult, no continental cognate, and no existence outside the Eddic record: he belongs to the North's own eschatological machinery. Scholars have long noted that the doubling of the apocalyptic wolf — one chasing the sun, one the moon — is probably a secondary systematization of the older single figure, the bound [[fenrir|Fenrir]] who breaks loose at the world's end; Simek and Lindow treat [[skoll|Skǫll]] and Hati as elaborations within the Fenrir-complex rather than as independent tradition, and [[garmr|Garmr]], the blood-caked hound of Gnipahellir who bays loose at Ragnarǫk, belongs to the same kennel.[^1]

What the pair does uniquely well is etiology. The devouring-monster account of eclipses is a comparative commonplace across cultures; the Norse version is distinctive for giving its monsters names, a pedigree, and a date. The chase gives the sky a reason for its haste — Sól hurries because Skǫll is behind her — and the wolf drawing near gives the medieval North its explanation of the eclipse: when the pursuer closes on [[mani|Máni]], the moon darkens.[^2]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hati, Skǫll, Garm; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sköll, Fenrir.
Orchard, Andy, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Hati, Sköll.

cultural-legacy.body:
Hati's afterlife is the eclipse-wolf's: wherever the Ragnarǫk story is retold, the pair [[skoll|Skǫll]] and Hati run in the sky above it. The nineteenth-century myth handbooks that introduced Norse cosmology to English readers made the chase a set-piece of mythological explanation — the sky's motions as a hunt, the eclipse as the moment the wolf gains — and every modern retelling of [[ragnarok|Ragnarǫk]], from children's mythologies to novels and games, keeps the two wolves as the ending's outriders.[^1]

In scholarship the name is the standing example of the Edda's transparent theonymy: a figure called, without ornament, 'the Hater'. Unlike Baldr or Freyja, the name never entered the living Scandinavian name-pool; it survives where it was born, in the poetry and its commentaries, doing the one job it was given.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sköll; Orchard, Andy, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Hati.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hati.

archaeology.body:
Hati is a wholly textual figure: no runestone names him, no votive deposit invokes him, and no image can be securely assigned to him.[^1] Wolf iconography is plentiful in the Viking-Age record — the wolf-riders and great-wolf scenes on the Gotland picture stones have been argued over since Lindqvist, and Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa (c. 983) proves that wolf-mounted figures of myth were carved in pre-Christian halls — but no carving carries an inscription that ties a wolf to the moon-chase. The stones are witnesses to a world that knew wolves of myth, not to this wolf.[^2]

The name's true witnesses are the manuscripts: *Grímnismál* in the Codex Regius (c. 1270) and AM 748 I 4to, *Völuspá* in the Codex Regius and Hauksbók, and Gylfaginning in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister codices, all recording material centuries older. The þulur of Skáldskaparmál preserve Hati and Hróðvitnir among the poetic heiti for 'wolf' — the tradition's own file of the name.[^3]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sköll, Fenrir.
Lindqvist, Sune, Gotlands Bildsteine, 2 vols. (Stockholm: Wahlström & Widstrand, 1941–42).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur (wolf-heiti), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).

meditation.body:
Hati is the Edda's most economical idea: take the verb 'to hate', give it legs, and set it running after the light. There is no malice-scene, no dialogue, no character beyond the name — only pursuit. And that is the point. The Norse imagination looked at the most orderly thing in the world, the clockwork of sun and moon, and read it as flight: the lights hurry because something hates them and is coming.[^1]

Time itself becomes the distance still left between the wolf and the moon — every night [[mani|Máni]] escapes is a night the world continues. Hati asks the uncomfortable question the whole Ragnarǫk cycle asks: how do you keep the light moving, knowing exactly what follows it? The Edda's answer is the one it gives everywhere. You keep running. The chase is the world.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 12, trans. Faulkes (1987); Völuspá 39–40, trans. Larrington (2014).

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda knows Hati by exactly one verse, and it is enough. *Grímnismál* 39, in [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s catalogue of the cosmos, names the two wolves of the sky: [[skoll|Skǫll]] follows the bright-faced god to the sheltering wood, 'but the other is Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, who runs before the bright bride of heaven' — the wolf ahead of the sun, on the heels of the moon.[^1] The surrounding stanzas supply the chase's context: [[sol|Sól]]'s horses Árvakr and Alsviðr, the shield Svalinn held before the sun, and the whole machinery of a heaven in motion.

*Völuspá* contributes the brood and the ending. Its seeress sees the old giantess in the Ironwood breeding [[fenrir|Fenrir]]'s kind, 'and from all of them comes one in particular, a snatcher of the moon in a troll's skin', who gorges on the doomed and reddens the gods' dwellings — the *tungls tjúgari* the handbooks read as Hati in his Ragnarǫk guise.[^2] The same poem's eschatology supplies the frame: the sun turning black and the stars vanishing are the catch made visible. *Vafþrúðnismál* adds the moon's own pedigree — [[mani|Máni]], Mundilfœri's son, who 'journeys every day' and counts the years for men: the fleeing light the wolf was bred to follow.[^3]

sources.citation: Grímnismál 37–39 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Völuspá 39–40 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Vafþrúðnismál 23 (Mundilfœri's children) (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

prose-edda.body:
The Prose Edda is Hati's systematizer. Gylfaginning builds the sky first — Mundilfari's children Sól and Máni set to drive the horses of the sun and moon — and then, when Gangleri remarks that the sun hurries as if afraid, High One springs the trap the whole cosmology was set to hold: 'the one who seeks her is right behind her, and she has no other way out than to run'. Two wolves are named: [[skoll|Skǫll]], who will take the sun, and 'Hati Hróðvitnisson; he runs in front of her and wants to catch the moon — and that is what will happen'.[^1]

Snorri's craft deserves note: he takes Grímnismál's compressed verse — the wolf 'before the bright bride of heaven' — and reads its geometry, setting the moon-chaser ahead of the sun because the moon travels ahead of her. In the same chapter he adds Mánagarmr, the 'moon-hound', mightiest of the brood, who will swallow the moon and spatter the sky with blood; whether this is Hati renamed or a third wolf, the tradition leaves open.[^1] Gylfaginning 51 pays the debt: at Ragnarǫk the wolves' running ends in the catches foretold, and the sky goes dark.[^2] Elsewhere the Prose Edda keeps the name filed where skalds could find it: the þulur of Skáldskaparmál list Hati and Hróðvitnir among the heiti for 'wolf'.[^3]

Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 51, trans. Faulkes (1987).

runic-evidence.body:
The runic corpus contains no attestation of the wolf Hati. No runestone names him, no amulet invokes him, and no inscription yet found links a carving to the moon-chase — a silence he shares with the whole Fenrir-complex, whose figures belong to poetry and prophecy rather than to dedicatory practice.[^1]

What the runic record offers is orthographic, not cultic. In the Younger Futhark of the Viking Age the name would have been carved **ᚼᛅᛏᛁ** — h-a-t-i, four runes with none of the underspecification that complicates longer names; the rendering is a normalized reconstruction, since no Viking-Age carving of the name is known. The etymological raw material is equally plain: the verb *hata*, 'to hate', is common Germanic vocabulary, and the agent noun *hati* needs no poetic license to mean what the myth requires.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sköll, Fenrir.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. hata; Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. hati.

sagas.body:
Beyond the Eddas, Hati has no medieval narrative afterlife. The legendary sagas and the kings' sagas never stage him; no fornaldarsaga hero meets the moon-wolf, and Saxo Grammaticus, who retells so much of the gods' history as Danish prehistory, gives no corresponding figure. His medieval existence outside the mythological poems is that of a learned word: the þulur — the metrical name-lists the skalds used as a thesaurus — preserve Hati and Hróðvitnir among the heiti for 'wolf', which means the name circulated as raw material for verse long after its myth was fixed.[^1]

That afterlife is instructive. A skald composing a wolf-kenning could reach for 'Hati' and count on his audience hearing both the animal and the chase after [[mani|Máni]]; the theonym and the common noun folded into one another, exactly as the myth intended. The name's whole career — poem, prose systematization, þula — never left the written tradition, and never needed to.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur (wolf-heiti), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hati.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Hati** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius (Grímnismál) and the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (Gylfaginning), recording material centuries older.[^1] Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the Younger Futhark; no runic attestation of this name survives, so the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is the agent noun *hati* 'hater', formed on the verb *hata* 'to hate' — a weak-declension masculine, hence the final stem vowel and the absence of the nominative *-r*.
- In the Younger Futhark it would have been carved ᚼᛅᛏᛁ (h-a-t-i), four runes with no ambiguity.
- Normalized Old Norse orthography writes no diacritic in this name: the vowels are short, and every letter is plain ASCII.
- The Unicode restoration Hati therefore differs from the ASCII input only by capitalization — Tier 2 by the mechanical rule.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. hati.
